chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shazaan from Safwan from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar from Muhammad al-Halabi who said:

We lodged in a place, and between us and the Masjid was a dirty alleyway. So I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and he said: 'Where did you lodge?' I said: 'We lodged in the house of so-and-so.' He said: 'Between you and the Masjid is a dirty alleyway,' or we said to him: 'Between us and the Masjid is a dirty alleyway.' He said: 'There is no problem; the earth purifies one part of it with another.' I said: 'And the wet manure that I tread upon?' He said: 'The likes of that does not harm you.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no problem / It is permissible

ai.seo_question: Does treading on wet feces invalidate prayer or cause ritual impurity?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the distinction between the inherent impurity of feces and the ritual purity of the ground itself, ruling that treading on wet manure does not transfer impurity to one's feet. This establishes the principle of *tathir al-ard* (the earth's self-purification), a key concept in Shia fiqh for determining the validity of prayer when walking on soiled surfaces. The dialogue highlights the practical application of natural purification mechanisms in daily worship.
